title: Malaysia: Tunku Abdul Rahman and Negotiated Independence in 1957
abstract: This recipe covers the negotiated path to Malayan independence in 1957, centered on Tunku Abdul Rahman, the Alliance leadership, the London talks, the constitutional settlement, and the institutional shape of the new independent state.

sections.heading: From Alliance Politics to the Independence Demand
bullet_points: Tunku Abdul Rahman became the central public figure in the independence drive after the Alliance consolidated electoral legitimacy.
The topic begins with the postwar constitutional opening and the move from colonial consultation to formal self-rule demands.
The alliance between UMNO, MCA, and MIC is important because it gave the independence claim a cross-communal political base.
The benchmark should emphasize negotiation and coalition politics rather than a purely unilateral anti-colonial break.

sections.heading: Negotiations in London and Constitutional Bargaining
bullet_points: The 1956 London mission was the decisive negotiated step in the route to independence.
British agreement was tied to constitutional safeguards, orderly transfer, and confidence in local political leadership.
The Reid Commission process mattered because it translated the political settlement into a durable constitutional framework.
The benchmark should preserve the distinction between achieving independence and designing the constitutional state that followed.

sections.heading: The Independence Settlement of 1957
bullet_points: Independence was declared on 31 August 1957 and marked the end of British colonial rule in the Federation of Malaya.
Tunku Abdul Rahman became the first prime minister of an independent Malaya.
The Federal Constitution created a constitutional monarchy and established a parliamentary framework.
The benchmark should treat the declaration, the constitutional order, and the first cabinet as linked but distinct facts.

sections.heading: Coalition Politics and Multiethnic Legitimacy
bullet_points: The Alliance's cross-communal structure helped make independence politically credible inside the Federation of Malaya.
UMNO, MCA, and MIC mattered not only as parties but as coalition partners in a negotiated transfer of power.
The topic can mention Bahasa Melayu terms such as merdeka and Persekutuan Tanah Melayu without drifting into another language domain.
This section should show how negotiated independence depended on elite bargaining and broad electoral legitimacy at the same time.

source_notes: Official Malaysia government history pages support the public role of Tunku and the Alliance.
The section is intentionally limited to coalition politics before and during independence, not later interethnic policy debates.

sections.heading: Limits of the 1957 Topic Boundary
bullet_points: The recipe stops at the 1957 independence settlement and does not expand into the formation of Malaysia in 1963.
Later constitutional or federal developments belong to separate topics and should not be merged into this one.
The benchmark should emphasize stable, documentary facts that are easy to verify from official sources.
The narrative is complete when it explains how negotiation, constitutional drafting, and declaration came together in 1957.
